Appendix A Details for Design-Based Validation

Here we provide the derivations of the debiased score of Section 3.3. For ease of notation, we work in one domain and suppress its index. Here θ\theta is the domain mean and θ^HT\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}} the full-sample HT estimator, with variance dd. Our objective is to validate a candidate MM, where θ^M\hat{\theta}^{M} is its estimator computed from the full sample. We divide our sample into folds indexed by kk. For each fold, we construct an HT estimate θ^HT,(k)\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)} using the held-out fold kk, which is used for validation. We also construct the estimator θ^M,(−k)\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)} based on the remaining K−1K-1 folds. We denote the averaged value of these quantities across folds as θ¯HT\bar{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}} and θ¯M\bar{\theta}^{M}. Two sources of randomness are in play, which sample 𝒮\mathcal{S} is drawn and how it is split into folds. Every expectation below operates over both sources.

A.1 The Bias of the Naive Score

Write

eM,(−k)=θ^M,(−k)−θ,eHT,(k)=θ^HT,(k)−θe^{M,(-k)}=\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}-\theta,\qquad e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}=\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\theta

for the errors of the candidate and held-out HT estimate at fold kk. The target is the candidate’s mean squared error averaged over the folds,

MSE⁡(M)=1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k))2].\mathrm{MSE}(M)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,(e^{M,(-k)})^{2}\,\right].

The folds are drawn at random, so the error has the same distribution at every fold. The naive score replaces the unknown θ\theta by the held-out HT estimate, whose discrepancy from the candidate is the difference of the two errors,

Snaive​(M)=1K​∑k=1K(θ^M,(−k)−θ^HT,(k))2=1K​∑k=1K(eM,(−k)−eHT,(k))2.\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{naive}}(M)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\bigr)^{2}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(e^{M,(-k)}-e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\bigr)^{2}.

We first seek to show that the bias for this naive score is:

𝔼⁡[Snaive​(M)]−MSE⁡(M)=1K​∑k=1KVar⁡[θ^HT,(k)]−2K​∑k=1KCov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{naive}}(M)\,\right]-\mathrm{MSE}(M)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]-\frac{2}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right].
Proof.

Given the definition of the naive score as a difference of the two errors, we have

𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k)−eHT,(k))2]=𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k))2]+𝔼⁡[(eHT,(k))2]−2​𝔼​[eM,(−k)​eHT,(k)]\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(e^{M,(-k)}-e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\bigr)^{2}\,\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,(e^{M,(-k)})^{2}\,\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,(e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)})^{2}\,\right]-2\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{M,(-k)}\,e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right] (7)

where this is a per-fold quantity. Note the second term is simply the variance of the held-out HT estimate, since it is unbiased.

The last cross term can be simplified to

𝔼⁡[eM,(−k)​eHT,(k)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{M,(-k)}\,e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right] =Cov⁡[eM,(−k),eHT,(k)]+𝔼⁡[eM,(−k)]​𝔼​[eHT,(k)]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,e^{M,(-k)},\,e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{M,(-k)}\,\right]\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]
=Cov⁡[θ^M,(−k),θ^HT,(k)]+𝔼⁡[eM,(−k)]​𝔼​[eHT,(k)]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{M,(-k)}\,\right]\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]
=Cov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)]+𝔼⁡[eM,(−k)]⋅0.\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,e^{M,(-k)}\,\right]\cdot 0.

The second equality is due to θ\theta being a constant and the third equality results from the unbiasedness of the held-out HT estimate. Then (7) can be simplified to

𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k)−eHT,(k))2]=𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k))2]+Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)]−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(e^{M,(-k)}-e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\bigr)^{2}\,\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,(e^{M,(-k)})^{2}\,\right]+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right].

Thus, the expectation of the naive score is

𝔼​[Snaive​(M)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{naive}}(M)\,\right] =1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k)−eHT,(k))2]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(e^{M,(-k)}-e^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\bigr)^{2}\,\right]
=1K​∑k=1K(𝔼⁡[(eM,(−k))2]+Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)]−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\biggl(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,(e^{M,(-k)})^{2}\,\right]+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right]\biggr)
=MSE⁡(M)+1K​∑k=1KVar⁡[θ^HT,(k)]−2K​∑k=1KCov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)].\displaystyle=\mathrm{MSE}(M)+\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]-\frac{2}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right].

∎

Note that this bias breaks into two components when conditioned on the realized sample 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The variance of the held-out estimate splits as

Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)]\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right] =𝔼⁡[Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]]+Var⁡[𝔼⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]
=𝔼⁡[Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]]+Var⁡[θ^HT]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\,\right]
=𝔼⁡[Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]]+d.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]+d.

The first equality is the law of total variance. The second holds because, given the sample, each sampled unit lands in fold kk with probability 1/K1/K, which cancels the factor KK on its weight, so the held-out estimate has conditional mean θ^HT\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}.11 1 For the Hájek estimator, which divides by the sum of the weights rather than the domain size, this conditional mean and the fold average used in Appendix A.2 hold to first order, and exactly under simple random sampling within the domain with equal fold sizes. The covariance with the candidate splits in the same way,

Cov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)]\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right] =𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]
+Cov⁡[𝔼⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮],𝔼⁡[θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]\displaystyle\quad+\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right],\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]
=𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]+Cov[θ^HT,𝔼[θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]+\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right],

by the law of total covariance and the same conditional mean. Averaging the last term over the folds,

1K​∑k=1KCov⁡[θ^HT,𝔼⁡[θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]\displaystyle\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right] =Cov⁡[θ^HT,𝔼⁡[θ¯M∣𝒮]]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]
=Cov[θ^HT,θ¯M]−𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,θ¯M∣𝒮]]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]
=Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ¯M].\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right].

The first equality is linearity, the second is the law of total covariance for θ¯M\bar{\theta}^{M}, and the third holds because θ^HT\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}} is fixed given the sample. Substituting the three results into the bias of the naive score,

𝔼⁡[Snaive​(M)]−MSE⁡(M)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{naive}}(M)\,\right]-\mathrm{MSE}(M)
=1K​∑k=1KVar⁡[θ^HT,(k)]−2K​∑k=1KCov⁡[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\right]-\frac{2}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\right]
=1K​∑k=1K{𝔼⁡[Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]]+d}\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]+d\Bigr\}
−2K∑k=1K{𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]+Cov[θ^HT,𝔼[θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]}\displaystyle\qquad\qquad-\frac{2}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl\{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]+\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]\Bigr\}
=1K∑k=1K𝔼[Var[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]]−2K∑k=1K𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]]⏟fold-level bias\displaystyle=\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]-\frac{2}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]}_{\text{fold-level bias}}
+d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ¯M]⏟sample-level bias.\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\underbrace{d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right]}_{\text{sample-level bias}}. (8)

In the last equality, we group the terms into fold-level and sample-level bias components. The fold-level bias comes from the random split of a fixed sample. The sample-level bias comes from the draw of the sample itself. Every held-out estimate centers on the full-sample HT estimate rather than on θ\theta, so the spread across the folds carries no information about it. We first examine the adjusted score of Dong and Li, (2026) that removes the fold-level bias.

A.2 The Adjusted Score

The fold-level bias above has two terms, the average conditional variance of the held-out estimates and their average conditional covariance with the candidate. The adjusted score of Dong and Li, (2026) estimates them by correcting the naive score,

Sadj​(M)=Snaive​(M)−υ^+2​c^M,\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{adj}}(M)=\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{naive}}(M)-\hat{\upsilon}+2\,\hat{c}^{M},

where υ^\hat{\upsilon} and c^M\hat{c}^{M} are defined by

υ^=1K​∑k=1K(θ^HT,(k)−θ¯HT)2,c^M=1K​∑k=1K(θ^HT,(k)−θ¯HT)​(θ^M,(−k)−θ¯M).\hat{\upsilon}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\bar{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)^{2},\qquad\hat{c}^{M}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\bar{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}-\bar{\theta}^{M}\bigr).

We seek to show that

𝔼[υ^]=1K∑k=1K𝔼[Var[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]],𝔼[c^M]=1K∑k=1K𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\upsilon}\,\right]=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right],\qquad\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{c}^{M}\,\right]=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right].
Proof.

The proof uses two facts about the held-out HT estimates, which follow from how the folds are built. Write 𝒮(k)\mathcal{S}^{(k)} for the sampled units in fold kk, so that θ^HT,(k)=N−1​∑j∈𝒮(k)K​wj​yj\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}=N^{-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}^{(k)}}K\,w_{j}\,y_{j}. The first fact is that the held-out estimates average to the full-sample estimate,

θ¯HT=1K​∑k=1K1N​∑j∈𝒮(k)K​wj​yj=1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​yj=θ^HT,\bar{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}^{(k)}}K\,w_{j}\,y_{j}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,y_{j}=\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}, (9)

where the second equality cancels the factor KK and uses that each sampled unit sits in exactly one fold. The second fact is that, given the sample, each held-out estimate has conditional mean equal to the full-sample estimate,

𝔼⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]=1N​∑j∈𝒮K​wj​yj​P​(j∈𝒮(k)∣𝒮)=1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​yj=θ^HT,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}K\,w_{j}\,y_{j}\,P\bigl(j\in\mathcal{S}^{(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\bigr)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,y_{j}=\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}, (10)

where the first equality takes the expectation over the split with the weights and labels fixed, and the second uses that each sampled unit lands in fold kk with probability 1/K1/K.

Given the sample, the expectation of υ^\hat{\upsilon} is

𝔼⁡[υ^∣𝒮]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\upsilon}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right] =1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[(θ^HT,(k)−θ¯HT)2∣𝒮]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\bar{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)^{2}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]
=1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)2∣𝒮]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)^{2}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]
=1K​∑k=1KVar⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right].

The first equality is linearity of conditional expectation, and the second uses (9). The third uses (10), since a squared deviation from the conditional mean has conditional expectation equal to the conditional variance.

The expectation of c^M\hat{c}^{M} takes two steps. First, the candidate’s fold average θ¯M\bar{\theta}^{M} drops out,

𝔼⁡[c^M∣𝒮]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{c}^{M}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right] =𝔼⁡[1K​∑k=1K(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)​(θ^M,(−k)−θ¯M)∣𝒮]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}-\bar{\theta}^{M}\bigr)\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]
=𝔼⁡[1K​∑k=1K(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)​θ^M,(−k)−θ¯M​1K​∑k=1K(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)|𝒮]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\biggl[\,\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}-\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\Bigm|\mathcal{S}\,\biggr]
=1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)​θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right].

The first equality uses (9), and the second expands the product and takes θ¯M\bar{\theta}^{M}, which does not depend on kk, outside the second sum. The third holds because the second sum is θ¯HT−θ^HT\bar{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}, which is zero by (9).

Second, each summand is a conditional covariance. Write μ(k)=𝔼⁡[θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]\mu^{(k)}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right] for the conditional mean of the candidate’s fit, which is fixed given the sample. Then

𝔼⁡[(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)​θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right] =𝔼⁡[(θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT)​(θ^M,(−k)−μ(k))∣𝒮]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr)\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}-\mu^{(k)}\bigr)\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]
=Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮].\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right].

The first equality subtracts μ(k)\mu^{(k)}, which changes nothing because μ(k)\mu^{(k)} is fixed given the sample and θ^HT,(k)−θ^HT\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}-\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}} has conditional mean zero by (10). The second holds because, by (10), both factors are deviations from their conditional means.

Finally, we average the two conditional expectations over samples,

𝔼⁡[υ^]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\upsilon}\,\right] =𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[υ^∣𝒮]]=1K​∑k=1K𝔼⁡[Var⁡[θ^HT,(k)∣𝒮]],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\upsilon}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right],
𝔼⁡[c^M]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{c}^{M}\,\right] =𝔼[𝔼[c^M∣𝒮]]=1K∑k=1K𝔼[Cov[θ^HT,(k),θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{c}^{M}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT},(k)},\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right].

In each line, the first equality is the law of total expectation, and the second substitutes the conditional expectation computed above. ∎

The adjusted score is therefore left with the sample-level bias,

𝔼⁡[Sadj​(M)]−MSE⁡(M)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{adj}}(M)\,\right]-\mathrm{MSE}(M) =d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ¯M]\displaystyle=d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right]
=d⁡(1−2​ρ),\displaystyle=d\,(1-2\rho),

where ρ=Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ¯M]/d\rho=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right]/d. The bias is zero only at ρ=1/2\rho=1/2. The HT estimator has ρ=1\rho=1, so its adjusted score is too low by dd. A candidate that uses no labels has ρ=0\rho=0, so its adjusted score is too high by dd.

A.3 The Debiased Score

The sample-level bias is d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ¯M]d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right], which involves the average of the candidate’s KK training fits, while the debiased score of Section 3.3 uses the full-sample fit θ^M\hat{\theta}^{M}. We assume that, given the sample, each training fit centers on the full-sample fit up to a remainder of order n−1n^{-1}, with nn the size of the whole sample,

𝔼⁡[θ^M,(−k)∣𝒮]=θ^M+Op​(n−1).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{M,(-k)}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]=\hat{\theta}^{M}+O_{p}\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr). (11)

Dong and Li, (2026) derive this approximation for the difference of two candidates from a linearization condition, and we assume it for a single candidate. Under this assumption,

d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ¯M]\displaystyle d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\right] =d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,𝔼⁡[θ¯M∣𝒮]]\displaystyle=d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\bar{\theta}^{M}\,\mid\,\mathcal{S}\,\right]\,\right]
=d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ^M+Op​(n−1)]\displaystyle=d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}^{M}+O_{p}\bigl(n^{-1}\bigr)\,\right]
≈d−2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ^M].\displaystyle\approx d-2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}^{M}\,\right].

The first equality holds because θ^HT\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}} is fixed given the sample, and the second averages (11) over the folds. Subtracting this sample-level bias from the adjusted score gives the debiased score (6),

Sdeb​(M)=Sadj​(M)−d+2​Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ^M].\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{deb}}(M)=\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{adj}}(M)-d+2\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}^{M}\,\right].

A.4 The Covariance for Each Candidate

The debiased score needs dd and the covariance Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ^M]\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}^{M}\,\right], and only the covariance depends on the candidate. Both are computed from the full sample.

HT.

When the candidate is the HT estimator itself, the covariance is its variance dd, so the debiased score adds −d+2​d=d-d+2d=d to the adjusted score.

PPI and GREG.

Both estimators are a known constant plus a weighted mean of residuals,

θ^M=1N​∑j∈𝒰pj+1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​rj,\hat{\theta}^{M}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}}p_{j}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,r_{j},

where pjp_{j} is the prediction, equal to fjf_{j} under PPI and λ^​fj\hat{\lambda}f_{j} under GREG, and rj=yj−pjr_{j}=y_{j}-p_{j} is the residual. With λ^\hat{\lambda} treated as fixed, the first term is a constant, so

Cov⁡[θ^HT,θ^M]\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}^{M}\,\right] =Cov⁡[1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​yj,1N​∑j∈𝒰pj+1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​rj]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,y_{j},\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}}p_{j}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,r_{j}\,\right]
=Cov⁡[1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​yj,1N​∑j∈𝒮wj​rj].\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,y_{j},\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,r_{j}\,\right].

The first equality writes out both estimators, and the second drops the constant. The result is the covariance between the weighted means of the labels and of the residuals. It is not the candidate’s own variance, which would have the residuals in place of the labels in the first argument.

Both dd and this covariance are estimated from the full sample by the linearization estimator for a weighted mean,

d^\displaystyle\hat{d} =nn−1​∑j∈𝒮wj2​(1−πj)​(yj−y¯)2(∑j∈𝒮wj)2,\displaystyle=\frac{n}{n-1}\,\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}^{2}\,(1-\pi_{j})\,(y_{j}-\bar{y})^{2}}{\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\bigr)^{2}},
Cov^​(θ^HT,θ^M)\displaystyle\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}\bigl(\hat{\theta}^{\mathrm{HT}},\hat{\theta}^{M}\bigr) =nn−1​∑j∈𝒮wj2​(1−πj)​(yj−y¯)​(rj−r¯)(∑j∈𝒮wj)2,\displaystyle=\frac{n}{n-1}\,\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}^{2}\,(1-\pi_{j})\,(y_{j}-\bar{y})(r_{j}-\bar{r})}{\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\bigr)^{2}},

where nn is the domain’s sample size, y¯=∑j∈𝒮wj​yj/∑j∈𝒮wj\bar{y}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,y_{j}/\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j} is the weighted mean of the labels, and r¯=∑j∈𝒮wj​rj/∑j∈𝒮wj\bar{r}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j}\,r_{j}/\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}w_{j} is the weighted mean of the residuals. The covariance estimator replaces one of the two centered labels in d^\hat{d} by a centered residual. The factor 1−πj1-\pi_{j} is the finite-population correction, and n/(n−1)n/(n-1) is the small-sample factor.

Smoothers.

A smoother uses every domain, so we bring back the domain index and write ziz_{i} for the input of domain ii. Once 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and the variance parameters are fixed (σ2\sigma^{2} under FH and PP-S, and σr2\sigma_{r}^{2} under TFH and PP-TS), each of the four smoothers is 𝑨​𝒛\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z} plus a term that does not depend on 𝒛\boldsymbol{z}, for a matrix 𝑨\boldsymbol{A} that we treat as fixed. Then

Cov⁡[θ^iHT,θ^iM]\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}\,\right] =Cov⁡[θ^iHT,∑l=1mAi​l​zl]\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\sum_{l=1}^{m}A_{il}\,z_{l}\,\right]
=∑l=1mAi​l​Cov⁡[θ^iHT,zl]\displaystyle=\sum_{l=1}^{m}A_{il}\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,z_{l}\,\right]
=Ai​i​Cov⁡[θ^iHT,zi].\displaystyle=A_{ii}\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,z_{i}\,\right].

The first equality writes out row ii of 𝑨​𝒛\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z} and drops the constant term, and the second is bilinearity with 𝑨\boldsymbol{A} fixed. The third holds because sampling errors of the direct estimates are independent across domains.

The coefficient Ai​iA_{ii} has a closed form. Stacking the domains, the four smoothers of Section 3.2 share the form

𝒛∣𝜽∼N(𝜽,𝑫),𝜽=𝑿𝜷+𝒗,𝒗∼N(𝟎,𝑮),\boldsymbol{z}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim N\!\left(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{D}\right),\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{v},\qquad\boldsymbol{v}\sim N\!\left(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{G}\right),

where 𝑫=diag⁡{Var⁡[z1],…,Var⁡[zm]}\boldsymbol{D}=\operatorname{diag}\{\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{1}\,\right],\dots,\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{m}\,\right]\} holds the sampling variances of the inputs, 𝑿\boldsymbol{X} stacks the covariates, and 𝑮\boldsymbol{G} is the covariance of the random effects. Given 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta}, the sampling error 𝒛−𝜽\boldsymbol{z}-\boldsymbol{\theta} is independent of 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, so CovM⁡[𝜽,𝒛]=𝑮\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\boldsymbol{\theta},\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]=\boldsymbol{G} and VarM⁡[𝒛]=𝑮+𝑫\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]=\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D}, and conditioning on 𝒛\boldsymbol{z} gives

𝑨\displaystyle\boldsymbol{A} =𝑮​(𝑮+𝑫)−1,\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D})^{-1},
VarM⁡[𝜽∣𝒛]\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right] =𝑮−𝑮​(𝑮+𝑫)−1​𝑮\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{G}-\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D})^{-1}\boldsymbol{G}
=𝑮​(𝑮+𝑫)−1​(𝑮+𝑫)−𝑮​(𝑮+𝑫)−1​𝑮\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D})-\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D})^{-1}\boldsymbol{G}
=𝑮​(𝑮+𝑫)−1​(𝑮+𝑫−𝑮)\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D})^{-1}\bigl(\boldsymbol{G}+\boldsymbol{D}-\boldsymbol{G}\bigr)
=𝑨​𝑫.\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{D}.

Because 𝑫\boldsymbol{D} is diagonal, the ii-th diagonal entry gives Ai​i=VarM⁡[θi∣𝒛]/Var⁡[zi]A_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\theta_{i}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]/\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right], so

Cov⁡[θ^iHT,θ^iM]=VarM⁡[θi∣𝒛]​Cov⁡[θ^iHT,zi]Var⁡[zi].\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}\,\right]=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\theta_{i}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]\,\frac{\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,z_{i}\,\right]}{\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]}.

Under FH and TFH the input is the HT estimate, so the ratio is one and the covariance is the posterior variance. Under PP-S and PP-TS the input is the GREG estimate. The numerator of the ratio is then the GREG covariance above, and the denominator is the GREG variance already supplied to the smoother.

The derivation above holds the variance parameters fixed. The implementation instead fits each smoother by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which integrates over them, so the smoothed estimate is no longer of the form 𝑨​𝒛\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{z} plus a constant. A first-order expansion of θ^iM\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M} in the inputs takes the place of that linear form, and the covariance chain above becomes

Cov⁡[θ^iHT,θ^iM]\displaystyle\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}\,\right] ≈∑l=1m∂θ^iM∂zl​Cov⁡[θ^iHT,zl]\displaystyle\approx\sum_{l=1}^{m}\frac{\partial\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}}{\partial z_{l}}\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,z_{l}\,\right]
=∂θ^iM∂zi​Cov⁡[θ^iHT,zi].\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}}{\partial z_{i}}\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,z_{i}\,\right].

This is the earlier chain with Ai​lA_{il} replaced by ∂θ^iM/∂zl\partial\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}/\partial z_{l}, and the equality again uses the independence of the sampling errors across domains. With the variance parameters fixed, ∂θ^iM/∂zi=Ai​i\partial\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}/\partial z_{i}=A_{ii} and the two chains coincide.

To find the derivative, note that θ^iM=𝔼M​[θi∣𝒛]\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\theta_{i}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right] is a posterior mean, and apply Tweedie’s formula (Efron,, 2011). Under the normal sampling model and any prior on 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, including one that integrates over the variance parameters, the formula and its companion for the posterior variance are

θ^iM=zi+Var⁡[zi]​∂ℓ⁡(𝒛)∂zi,VarM⁡[θi∣𝒛]=Var⁡[zi]+Var⁡[zi]2​∂2ℓ⁡(𝒛)∂zi2,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}=z_{i}+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]\,\frac{\partial\ell(\boldsymbol{z})}{\partial z_{i}},\qquad\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\theta_{i}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]=\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]^{2}\,\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{z})}{\partial z_{i}^{2}},

where ℓ⁡(𝒛)\ell(\boldsymbol{z}) is the log density of the inputs under the model. The first follows from differentiating ℓ\ell once in ziz_{i}, which brings down the posterior mean of θi−zi\theta_{i}-z_{i}. Differentiating a second time brings down its posterior second moment, and subtracting the square of the first derivative leaves the posterior variance, which gives the second. Differentiating the first,

∂θ^iM∂zi\displaystyle\frac{\partial\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}}{\partial z_{i}} =1+Var⁡[zi]​∂2ℓ⁡(𝒛)∂zi2\displaystyle=1+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]\,\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{z})}{\partial z_{i}^{2}}
=1Var⁡[zi]​(Var⁡[zi]+Var⁡[zi]2​∂2ℓ⁡(𝒛)∂zi2)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]}\biggl(\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]+\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]^{2}\,\frac{\partial^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{z})}{\partial z_{i}^{2}}\biggr)
=VarM⁡[θi∣𝒛]Var⁡[zi],\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\theta_{i}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]}{\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]},

where the second equality factors out 1/Var⁡[zi]1/\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right], and the third recognizes the term in parentheses as the posterior variance from the companion formula. Substituting into the first-order chain gives

Cov⁡[θ^iHT,θ^iM]≈VarM⁡[θi∣𝒛]Var⁡[zi]​Cov⁡[θ^iHT,zi],\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{M}\,\right]\approx\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{M}}\!\left[\,\theta_{i}\,\mid\,\boldsymbol{z}\,\right]}{\operatorname{Var}\!\left[\,z_{i}\,\right]}\,\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[\,\hat{\theta}_{i}^{\mathrm{HT}},\,z_{i}\,\right],

the same formula as in the fixed case, with the posterior variance now computed from the retained draws.

Appendix B Additional Details for the Benchmark Simulation

We merge the MATH task types on advanced subjects into one domain and exclude one task type on which phi-4 answers every question correctly, leaving 34 task types with NiN_{i} from 146 to 670, median 250. Labels are drawn by SRS without replacement within each domain, so πi​j=ni/Ni\pi_{ij}=n_{i}/N_{i} and the variance of the HT estimator is estimated by

di=(1−niNi)​si2ni,d_{i}\;=\;\Bigl(1-\frac{n_{i}}{N_{i}}\Bigr)\frac{s_{i}^{2}}{n_{i}},

with si2s_{i}^{2} the sample variance of the labels in 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}. PPI and GREG use the same expression on their residuals. Every smoother is fit by Gibbs sampling with one chain, keeping 2,000 draws after a burn-in of 1,000 iterations. FH and PP-S are fit on the original scale under the flat prior on 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and σ2\sigma^{2}. For TFH and PP-TS the inputs ziz_{i} are standardized by the mean and standard deviation of the observed inputs, with did_{i} scaled to match, and each coefficient in 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} then has a N⁡(0,104)N\!\left(0,10^{4}\right) prior and each level variance σr2\sigma_{r}^{2} an inverse-gamma prior with shape 3 and scale 0.6. The point estimate is the posterior mean, and the 95% interval runs from the 2.5% to the 97.5% posterior quantile.

The compilation of Wu et al., (2026) sorts about 4,400 models by release date and takes the earlier half, about 2,200 models, as historical. All three auxiliaries are built from that half alone, and phi-4 and every model fine-tuned from it fall in the newer half.

The same 100 samples serve every estimator and every auxiliary, so the rows of the estimators that use no auxiliary repeat exactly across the three auxiliary blocks. A domain whose sampled labels all agree has an estimated variance of zero and is left out of every estimator’s metrics in that replication; this affects 0.6 domains on average across the 100 replications at 10%, 0.1 at 20% and none at 30%. Tables 5, 6 and 7 report RMSE, interval score and coverage at all three sampling budgets and under all three auxiliaries, with each smoother twice, once with intercept-only linking and once with the auxiliary’s domain mean as covariate. At a matched linking model the smoother on the GREG input is never worse than the same smoother on the HT input, under any auxiliary at any budget and paired within replication.

Appendix C Additional Details for the Agent Traffic Analysis

C.1 The PRISM Data

We use the PRISM dataset (Kirk et al.,, 2024), which records human ratings on every response to an LLM prompt. The dataset is large enough to sample from, and we treat it as the traffic of a deployed AI system. In PRISM, a participant’s opening prompt is sent to up to four LLMs, and the participant rates every response and chooses one LLM to continue the conversation with. Each later turn returns two responses from the chosen LLM, which the participant again rates before choosing one. Every rated response is a unit, so one conversation contributes several units to the population. The content covariates are recorded for every response, whether or not its rating is sampled:

  • •

    the log of the response’s length in characters,

  • •

    an indicator that the response answers the opening prompt,

  • •

    an indicator that the participant chose the response.

The traffic analysis also uses the score of an LLM judge, described in the next subsection.

In the traffic analysis of the Results, ratings are drawn by stratified SRS, so the chance that a response is sampled depends only on its domain. Whether the participant chose a response therefore plays no part in which ratings are sampled, and the chosen indicator enters only as a covariate.

The demonstration in Section 2 instead uses informative selection, in which the chance that a response is sampled depends on something related to its rating. Participants rate the responses they choose far higher, 81.7 on average against 54.1 for the rest. Each response is sampled independently with probability proportional to exp⁡(t​z)\exp(tz), where zz is the standardized chosen indicator and t=−0.30t=-0.30, scaled so that the expected sample size meets the budget. A chosen response is therefore sampled at 0.54 times the rate of a rejected one, which puts the correlation between being sampled and the rating at about 0.03 in magnitude at the 5% budget. The judge is nearly blind to this choice. The judge’s scores differ by about 5 points between chosen and rejected responses, while the participants’ ratings differ by about 28.

C.2 The Judge

The traffic judge is gpt-5-nano at low reasoning effort, prompted zero-shot to predict the participant’s own 1 to 100 rating of the final response. Each conversation is submitted in full, with the response to score marked and no participant attributes included, and the judge returns a score and a confidence as structured output. The prompt was written once and frozen before any scoring:

You will see a conversation between a user and an AI assistant. The conversation ends with an assistant response marked for scoring. Immediately after that response, the user rated it on a scale from 1 to 100, where higher means they were more satisfied with it. Predict the score the user gave. Judge the response from that user’s perspective in the context of the conversation, not against an external standard of quality.

Reply with JSON:
{"score": <integer 1-100>, "confidence": <integer 0-100>}
where confidence is how sure you are of the prediction.

Scoring all 68,371 responses cost about six dollars.

C.3 Results at the 20% Budget

Tables 8 and 9 repeat the traffic study’s comparisons at the 20% budget, 13,674 ratings, alongside the 10% columns of the main text. Domain sizes NiN_{i} run from 423 to 1,809, median 1,129. Every conclusion carries over: the oracle ordering of the candidates is unchanged, the two one-sample scores and the even split remain equivalent on the choice, and only DB-CV reports a calibrated error. Table 8 also reports each candidate’s interval score and coverage against the oracle. Coverage sits between 0.943 and 0.964 against the nominal 95% level for every candidate, and the interval-score gains track the RMSE gains.
